Source: Augmented intelligent distributed sensing system model for precision agriculture
Abstract: Over the past years, augmented intelligence inspired by natural evolution evolved to the implementation of algorithm models that combine Artificial Intelligence techniques supported by human interactions and sensor data integration, providing new ways to look to the existing data and transform it into valuable outputs for areas that before were difficult to introduce innovation and technology. Agriculture is one of the oldest activities, but its evolution has not kept up with human needs. In order to increase production and ensure its sustainability, it is necessary to move towards precision agriculture. This work will explore some of the latest developments in the area of network and sensor information and was motivated by the interests shown by a consortium that includes Globaltronic, Quinta do Crasto and Altice Labs in improving the existing weather stations to assist the irrigation process since this demands the precise knowledge of the amount of water that is to be supplied to the plants. To achieve this, we need to use reliable measuring systems for water but also for the number of chemical agents, like fertilizers, that contribute to the growth of the plants, but impacts also to the pollution of rivers and water supplies.
Methods: Conceptual paper exploring recent developments in network and sensor information for precision agriculture. It is motivated by a consortium interest in improving weather stations for irrigation and chemical-agent monitoring; no formal method is described.
Results: No empirical results are reported in the abstract. The paper states that precision agriculture needs reliable measuring systems for water and chemical agents to support irrigation and reduce pollution.
Conclusions: Improving sensor-based measurement systems is presented as necessary for sustainable precision agriculture and better irrigation decisions. The abstract does not state specific limitations.

Source: Livestock Monitoring Based on Microclimate and Behavior Tracking Sensors: A Systematic Review
Abstract: Sensor-based cattle monitoring is a growing field within precision livestock farming, where machine learning algorithms are used to detect health issues, monitor behavior, and improve productivity. However, the diversity of evaluation strategies, performance metrics, and algorithmic choices in the current literature complicates comparison and selection of machine learning models. In this study, we conduct a systematic review and quantitative analysis of machine learning approaches applied to sensor-driven cattle monitoring tasks. We evaluate and compare algorithms using a broad spectrum of performance indicators, including accuracy, F1-score, precision, and recall, alongside their variability across studies. Through detailed heatmap visualizations and statistical summaries (mean, median, standard deviation, coefficient of variation), we identify the most consistently high-performing models and the factors contributing to variability. Results show that Convolutional Neural Networks and Extreme Gradient Boosting achieve the highest F1-scores and most balanced precision-recall performance, especially in imbalanced health detection tasks, while tree ensemble models such as Random Forest and Gradient Boosting demonstrate superior accuracy and consistency for behavior classification on balanced datasets. Our findings emphasize the importance of multi-metric evaluation frameworks and context-aware algorithm selection in the development of scalable and reliable livestock monitoring systems.
Methods: Systematic review and quantitative analysis of machine learning approaches for sensor-driven cattle monitoring, using heatmap visualizations and statistical summaries (mean, median, standard deviation, coefficient of variation).
Results: CNNs and XGBoost achieved the highest F1-scores and most balanced precision-recall performance, especially for imbalanced health detection tasks. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting showed superior accuracy and consistency for behavior classification on balanced datasets.
Conclusions: Multi-metric evaluation frameworks and context-aware algorithm selection are important for scalable, reliable livestock monitoring systems.

Source: Dynamic characterization of explanations during human–machine collaboration in cyber-physical systems
Abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems often rely on human–machine collaboration to achieve superior outcomes and mutual learning. For effective collaboration, systems must be understandable and trustworthy. Explanations are instrumental in promoting system understandability and building human trust. However, crafting such explanations poses key challenges: How many explanations do users need? How much information can they process? What level of detail is appropriate? This work introduces a conceptual model to characterize explanations and a predictive model that determines when and what type of explanation to provide. The predictive model considers system context, user profile, and interaction behavior, using machine learning techniques to infer explanatory needs and tailor responses accordingly. Although we apply our approach to a smart home environment, the methodology is generalizable to other CPS domains. At design time, developers define possible explanation points and relevant parameters. At runtime, the system autonomously adapts explanations to user-specific conditions. To validate our proposal, we conducted an experimental study evaluating the resulting explanations in terms of understandability, obtrusiveness, and adaptability. Results showed modest but meaningful improvements in all three dimensions, suggesting that our framework facilitates explanation designs more aligned with user preferences and situational demands.
Methods: Conceptual model plus predictive machine-learning model for tailoring explanations using system context, user profile, and interaction behavior. Validated in an experimental study in a smart home CPS setting.
Results: Experimental study found modest but meaningful improvements in understandability, obtrusiveness, and adaptability.
Conclusions: The framework appears to better align explanation design with user preferences and situational demands. It was demonstrated in a smart home environment, so broader generalization remains to be established.

Source: Collaborative Human in the Loop Robotics Framework for Precision Agriculture and Crop Monitoring
Abstract: This paper presents a Collaborative Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Robotics Framework of precision agriculture and crop monitoring, which tries to bring together the benefits of human decision-making and robotic efficiency. The HITL framework is developed to overcome the drawbacks of the conventional autonomous systems, where real-time human input is included to enhance flexibility, precision, and adaptability to the dynamic agricultural conditions. The technology uses autonomous robots having sensors, like RGB cameras, thermal sensors, and soil moisture sensors, to check the state of crops, pest infestation, and irrigation. The data gathered is processed by AI algorithms, and human operators are involved when complicated decisions are required, giving feedback to guide robots. Early experiments of the framework in actual farm environments demonstrated good performance with an accuracy of crop yield prediction of 92 %, pest detection of 89 %, and water use efficiency of 94 %, which were much better than the conservativeness of robotic systems used traditionally. The HITL framework also displayed the balance between autonomy and human competency by low frequency of human interventions (10% of the tasks) and high effectiveness of interventions (80%). The results also show how HITL framework can improve precision farming by enhancing the accuracy of crop monitoring, reducing the waste of resources, and increasing the productivity. The flexibility of the system to fluctuating environments renders it a useful resource to the contemporary agriculture industry. Future studies have the potential to investigate more sophisticated AI solutions like deep learning to make decisions in real-time and evaluate how the framework may be scaled to different agricultural areas and crops.
Methods: Collaborative human-in-the-loop robotics framework for precision agriculture and crop monitoring using autonomous robots with RGB, thermal, and soil moisture sensors plus AI processing and human feedback. Early experiments were conducted in actual farm environments.
Results: Crop yield prediction accuracy was 92%, pest detection 89%, and water use efficiency 94%. Human interventions were needed for 10% of tasks, with 80% effectiveness.
Conclusions: The HITL framework improved crop monitoring accuracy, reduced resource waste, and increased productivity. Future work should test more advanced AI for real-time decisions and scaling across agricultural areas and crops.

Source: Data Augmentation On-the-fly and Active Learning in Data Stream Classification
Abstract: There is an emerging need for predictive models to be trained on-the-fly, since in numerous machine learning applications data are arriving in an online fashion. A critical challenge encountered is that of limited availability of ground truth information (e.g., labels in classification tasks) as new data are observed one-by-one online, while another significant challenge is that of class imbalance. This work introduces the novel Augmented Queues method, which addresses the dual-problem by combining in a synergistic manner online active learning, data augmentation, and a multi-queue memory to maintain separate and balanced queues for each class. We perform an extensive experimental study using image and time-series augmentations, in which we examine the roles of the active learning budget, memory size, imbalance level, and neural network type. We demonstrate two major advantages of Augmented Queues. First, it does not reserve additional memory space as the generation of synthetic data occurs only at training times. Second, learning models have access to more labelled data without the need to increase the active learning budget and / or the original memory size. Learning on-the-fly poses major challenges which, typically, hinder the deployment of learning models. Augmented Queues significantly improves the performance in terms of learning quality and speed. Our code is made publicly available.
Methods: Novel Augmented Queues method for online data-stream classification, combining active learning, on-the-fly data augmentation, and a multi-queue memory. Experimental study used image and time-series augmentations and varied active learning budget, memory size, imbalance level, and neural network type.
Results: Augmented Queues improved learning quality and speed. It provided more labeled data without increasing active learning budget or original memory size.
Conclusions: The method addresses limited labels and class imbalance in online learning and is suitable for learning on-the-fly. A key advantage is that synthetic data are generated only at training time, so no extra memory is reserved.

Source: A Hybrid of Interactive Learning and Predictive Modeling for Occupancy Estimation in Smart Buildings
Abstract: This paper proposes a statistical learning approach for estimating occupancy in smart buildings using a set of small and simple nonintrusive sensors that can be viewed as alternatives to sensors that are sometimes perceived as invasive such as cameras. In that context, large amount of labelled training data are required. However, labelling large scale occupancy data is time consuming and tedious since it requires the direct involvement of the users. To tackle this challenge, we consider a hybrid approach based on the recently introduced interactive learning methodology that allows to collect training data of good quality, by ensuring a minimal involvement of the user, and a classification approach that we have developed. The classification part is based on the predictive distribution of the generalized Dirichlet (GD) mixture model which unfortunately does not have a closed-form. To alleviate that issue, we calculate a reliable approximation to the predictive distribution by optimizing the parameters of GD posterior distribution by a Bayesian variational inference approach. The choice of the GD mixture model is motivated by the heterogeneous non-Gaussian nature of the sensors outputs. Extensive experimental results reported for both synthetic data and real data indicate that our method could achieve promising results especially with extremely small training data.
Methods: Hybrid interactive learning and predictive modeling for occupancy estimation using small nonintrusive sensors. The classifier uses a generalized Dirichlet mixture model with Bayesian variational inference to approximate the predictive distribution.
Results: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real data showed promising occupancy estimation results, especially with extremely small training data.
Conclusions: The hybrid approach is effective for collecting good-quality training data with minimal user involvement and performs well under scarce-label conditions. A key limitation is that the generalized Dirichlet predictive distribution has no closed form and requires approximation.

Source: Deep learning-driven IoT solution for smart tomato farming
Abstract: The rising food demand and challenges with respect to the climate have made precision agriculture (PA) vital for sustainable crop production. This study presents an IoT-based smart greenhouse platform tailored for tomato farming, integrating environmental sensing and deep learning. The system employs ESP32-based wireless sensors to collect real-time data on soil moisture, temperature, and humidity; this data is transmitted to a cloud dashboard (ThingsBoard) for remote monitoring. A Raspberry Pi equipped with a Pi Camera and a YOLOv8 model classifies tomato ripeness stages—green, half-ripened, and fully ripened—using real greenhouse images. Model optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and TensorRT, improved inference speed by 35% while maintaining 52.8% classification accuracy during our initial stage of the project. Energy profiling revealed daily consumption of 8.91 Wh for the ESP32 sensors and 78 Wh for the Raspberry Pi. This prototype demonstrates real-time monitoring, high model precision, and practical energy insights, paving the way for multi-node scalability and edge AI enhancements. Future work will explore incorporating Edge TPU for faster on-device processing, LoRa for low-power, long-distance data transfer, and automated control of irrigation and ventilation systems to realize a fully autonomous smart greenhouse.
Methods: IoT-based smart greenhouse prototype for tomato farming using ESP32 wireless sensors, ThingsBoard cloud monitoring, and a Raspberry Pi with Pi Camera and YOLOv8 for ripeness classification. Model optimization used quantization, pruning, and TensorRT on real greenhouse images.
Results: Inference speed improved by 35% while maintaining 52.8% classification accuracy in the initial stage. Daily energy use was 8.91 Wh for the ESP32 sensors and 78 Wh for the Raspberry Pi.
Conclusions: The prototype enabled real-time monitoring, strong model precision, and practical energy profiling, supporting scalability and edge AI enhancements. Future work will add Edge TPU, LoRa, and automated irrigation and ventilation control.

Source: Artificial intelligence in environmental monitoring: in-depth analysis
Abstract: This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric and in-depth analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in environmental monitoring, based on 4762 publications from 1991 to 2024. The research highlights a notable increase in publications and citations since 2010, with China, the United States, and India emerging as leading contributors. Key areas of research include air and water quality monitoring, climate change modeling, biodiversity assessment, and disaster management. The integration of AI with emerging technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and remote sensing, has significantly expanded real-time environmental monitoring capabilities and data-driven decision-making. In-depth analysis reveals advancements in AI/ML methodologies, including novel algorithms for soil mapping, land-cover classification, flood susceptibility modeling, and remote sensing image analysis. Notable applications include enhanced air quality predictions, water quality assessments, climate impact forecasting, and automated wildlife monitoring using AI-driven image recognition. Challenges such as the “black-box” nature of AI models, the need for high-quality data in resource-constrained regions, and the complexity of real-time disaster management are also addressed. The study highlights ongoing efforts to develop explainable AI (XAI) models, which aim to improve model transparency and trust in critical environmental applications. Future research directions emphasize improving data quality and availability, fostering interdisciplinary collaborations across environmental and computer sciences, and addressing ethical considerations in AI-driven environmental management. These findings underscore the transformative potential of AI and ML technologies for sustainable environmental management, offering valuable insights for researchers and policymakers in addressing global environmental challenges.
Methods: Bibliometric and in-depth analysis of AI and machine learning applications in environmental monitoring, based on 4,762 publications from 1991 to 2024.
Results: Publication and citation counts have increased notably since 2010; China, the United States, and India are leading contributors. Key applications include air and water quality monitoring, climate modeling, biodiversity assessment, and disaster management.
Conclusions: AI and ML have transformative potential for sustainable environmental management, but challenges remain in model interpretability, data quality in resource-constrained regions, and real-time disaster management. Future work should improve data quality, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical oversight.

Source: Integrated Modeling Approaches for Agricultural Digital twins: the role of Process Based Models, Agent Based Models, Machine Learning, and Model Coupling
Abstract: Process-based models (PBMs) provide a mechanistic foundation for simulating complex genotype, environment, and management interactions across multiple scales. Integrating PBMs with agent-based models (ABMs), machine learning (ML), and advanced model coupling strategies (sequential, loose, tight, and framework-based) enables more comprehensive representations of agricultural systems. ABMs capture the adaptive behaviours of individual farmers, while ML techniques efficiently approximate nonlinear physiological processes or act as surrogates for computationally expensive submodules and reveal data-driven patterns, collectively enhancing the simulation of G × E × M interactions under variable climate scenarios. Digital twins (DTs), defined as systems that dynamically synchronize virtual models with real-time sensor data, extend coupled PBM–ABM–ML systems by enabling bidirectional feedback between computational models and farm operations. However, the implementation of DTs remains constrained by challenges such as data integration across heterogeneous sources, computational scalability, and semantic/technical interoperability making them appropriate only where continuous decision support and real-time feedback outweigh complexity and cost. This review evaluates the function of PBMs as the mechanistic core of DT architectures, surveys model integration techniques, and outlines the IT infrastructure required for operationalization. We conclude that digital twins are best deployed when real-time feedback is essential, whereas PBM–ABM–ML couplings suffice for research and policy applications requiring long-term scenario analysis.
Methods: Review article evaluating PBMs as the mechanistic core of digital twin architectures, surveying model integration techniques and IT infrastructure for operationalization. No formal search or quantitative method is described.
Results: PBMs, ABMs, ML, and coupling strategies can better represent G × E × M interactions and variable climate scenarios. Digital twins add bidirectional feedback with real-time sensor data, but are constrained by data integration, scalability, and interoperability challenges.
Conclusions: Digital twins are best deployed when real-time feedback is essential, while PBM–ABM–ML couplings are sufficient for research and policy applications needing long-term scenario analysis. Key limitations are heterogeneity of data sources, computational scalability, and semantic/technical interoperability.

Source: Human-Centered AI in Smart Farming: Toward Agriculture 5.0
Abstract: This paper delineates the contemporary landscape, challenges, and prospective developments in human-centred artificial intelligence (AI) within the ambit of smart farming, a pivotal element of the emergent Agriculture 5.0, supplanting Agriculture 4.0. Analogous to Industry 4.0, agriculture has witnessed a trend towards comprehensive automation, often marginalizing human involvement. However, this approach has encountered limitations in agricultural contexts for various reasons. While AI's capacity to assume human tasks is acknowledged, the inclusion of human expertise and experiential knowledge (human-in-the-loop) often proves indispensable, corroborated by the Moravec's Paradox: tasks simple for humans are complex for AI. Furthermore, social, ethical, and legal imperatives necessitate human oversight of AI, a stance strongly reflected in the European Union's regulatory framework. Consequently, this paper explores the advancements in human-centred AI focusing on their application in agricultural processes. These technological strides aim to enhance crop yields, minimize labor and resource wastage, and optimize the farm-to-consumer supply chain. The potential of AI to augment human decision-making, thereby fostering a sustainable, efficient, and resilient agri-food sector, is a focal point of this discussion - motivated by the current worldwide extreme weather events. Finally, a framework for Agriculture 5.0 is presented, which balances technological prowess with the needs, capabilities, and contexts of human stakeholders. Such an approach, emphasizing accessible, intuitive AI systems that meaningfully complement human activities, is crucial for the successful realization of future Agriculture 5.0.
Methods: Narrative overview of human-centred AI in smart farming and Agriculture 5.0; no formal search or empirical method is described. It presents a framework balancing technological capabilities with human stakeholder needs.
Results: Human-in-the-loop AI is presented as necessary in agriculture because automation has limitations, tasks simple for humans can be difficult for AI, and social, ethical, and legal oversight is required. The paper highlights potential benefits including higher yields, less labor and resource waste, and a more efficient supply chain.
Conclusions: Human-centred AI is portrayed as essential for Agriculture 5.0, with accessible and intuitive systems needed to complement human activities. A key limitation noted is that full automation can marginalize human expertise and face practical, regulatory, and contextual constraints.

Source: A Review of Intelligent Perception Technologies and Their Applications in Agricultural AGVs for Agricultural 5.0
Abstract: Agriculture 5.0 represents a breakthrough transformation from Agriculture 4.0, addressing the needs for safety, sustainability, and resilience in human–robot collaboration in agriculture. By integrating technologies such as artificial intelligence, digital twins, and big data, it achieves breakthroughs in three areas: perception, cognition, and execution. As carriers of agricultural technology, agricultural automated guided vehicles (AGVs) are an indispensable part of agricultural activities and play a crucial role in agricultural production. In the actual operation of AGVs, intelligent perception is a core technological prerequisite for enabling the communication and interaction among machines, humans, and the environment. However, due to the complexity and variability of agricultural environments, intelligent perception technology remains a highly challenging task. While existing reviews have focused on isolated aspects of agricultural automation, a comprehensive synthesis of intelligent perception technologies for agricultural AGVs within the holistic, human-centric framework of Agriculture 5.0 is notably lacking. This review bridges this gap by systematically analyzing and comprehensively reviewing recent advances in intelligent perception for agricultural AGVs, covering multi-sensor technologies, visual perception and target recognition, positioning and navigation algorithms, as well as applications such as path planning, multi-robot coordination, and human–robot collaboration. Furthermore, this paper delves into the potential challenges and future development trends of intelligent perception technology in the context of Agriculture 5.0, highlighting the transformative potential of these technologies in promoting multimodal fusion and addressing safety issues in human–robot collaboration. In the context of Agriculture 5.0, with the continuous advancement of intelligent perception technologies and the ongoing improvement of agricultural intelligent equipment, a human-centered, highly sustainable, resilient, data-driven agricultural production system will ultimately be formed in the future.
Methods: Narrative review systematically analyzing recent advances in intelligent perception for agricultural AGVs under the Agriculture 5.0 framework. Covers multi-sensor technologies, visual perception and target recognition, positioning and navigation algorithms, path planning, multi-robot coordination, and human–robot collaboration.
Results: The review identifies intelligent perception as a core prerequisite for AGV communication and interaction in complex agricultural environments. It synthesizes advances across multimodal sensing, perception, navigation, and collaboration, and highlights multimodal fusion and safety in human–robot collaboration as key trends.
Conclusions: The paper concludes that intelligent perception technologies are essential for Agriculture 5.0 and will support a human-centered, sustainable, resilient, data-driven agricultural production system. A key challenge remains the complexity and variability of agricultural environments.

Source: Human-In-The-Loop: Role in Cyber Physical Agricultural Systems
Abstract: With increasing automation, the ‘human' element in industrial systems is gradually being reduced, often for the sake of standardization. Complete automation, however, might not be optimal in complex, uncertain environments due to the dynamic and unstructured nature of interactions. Leveraging human perception and cognition can prove fruitful in making automated systems robust and sustainable. “Human-in-the-loop” (HITL) systems are systems which incorporate meaningful human interactions into the workflow. Agricultural Robotic Systems (ARS), developed for the timely detection and prevention of diseases in agricultural crops, are an example of cyber-physical systems where HITL augmentation can provide improved detection capabilities and system performance. Humans can apply their domain knowledge and diagnostic skills to fill in the knowledge gaps present in agricultural robotics and make them more resilient to variability. Owing to the multi-agent nature of ARS, HUB-CI, a collaborative platform for the optimization of interactions between agents is emulated to direct workflow logic. The challenge remains in designing and integrating human roles and tasks in the automated loop. This article explains the development of a HITL simulation for ARS, by first realistically modeling human agents, and exploring two different modes by which they can be integrated into the loop: Sequential, and Shared Integration. System performance metrics such as costs, number of tasks, and classification accuracy are measured and compared for different collaboration protocols. The results show the statistically significant advantages of HUB-CI protocols over the traditional protocols for each integration, while also discussing the competitive factors of both integration modes. Strengthening human modeling and expanding the range of human activities within the loop can help improve the practicality and accuracy of the simulation in replicating a HITL-ARS.
Methods: Simulation study for agricultural robotic systems (ARS) with human agents realistically modeled and integrated via Sequential and Shared Integration modes in a HUB-CI collaborative platform. Performance metrics including costs, number of tasks, and classification accuracy were compared across collaboration protocols.
Results: HUB-CI protocols showed statistically significant advantages over traditional protocols for each integration mode. Costs, number of tasks, and classification accuracy were measured and compared, with competitive factors noted between the two integration modes.
Conclusions: Strengthening human modeling and expanding human activities in the loop can improve the practicality and accuracy of HITL-ARS simulation. The authors note a need to better design and integrate human roles and tasks in the automated loop.

Source: Smooth Human–Robot Shared Control for Autonomous Orchard Monitoring With UGVs
Abstract: Precision agriculture offers the opportunity to automate routine or difficult tasks in orchards and vineyards, such as spraying or inspection, with Uncrewed Ground Vehicles (UGV). In this context, human operators should be kept in the closed-loop control of the robot for safety and reliability. This work is motivated by the challenges of effectively deploying human-robot shared control in the field. First, an asymptotically stable controller keeps the robot on the desired trajectory between rows of trees, whose distance is on the order of the robot’s width. Second, the robot must efficiently avoid static and moving obstacles on its path. Third, the control inputs must not exceed the actuator limits, which can degrade trajectory tracking performance, cause instability, or damage critical hardware. Finally, in real-life scenarios, user intervention is sometimes required to manage unpredictable situations. To overcome these challenges, we propose and deploy a shared controller that continuously and smoothly varies the ratio of human and automatic control inputs depending on the human’s intent, geometrically rescales trajectory inputs to maintain bounded control, and incorporates obstacle avoidance capabilities – all while preserving asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system. Additionally, we introduce a time re-scaling strategy that modifies trajectory evolution, ensuring target positions remain within a defined vicinity of the robot. The system performance was assessed in simulation and in 26 field trials inside an apple orchard using different obstacle configurations, weather, and terrain conditions, with a success rate of 100% and an average tracking error of 0.1 m.
Methods: Shared human-robot controller for UGV orchard monitoring that smoothly varies human and automatic inputs, geometrically rescales trajectory inputs, adds obstacle avoidance, and uses time rescaling to preserve stability. Evaluated in simulation and 26 apple-orchard field trials under varying obstacles, weather, and terrain.
Results: Simulation and 26 field trials achieved a 100% success rate with an average tracking error of 0.1 m.
Conclusions: The proposed shared controller enabled safe, stable orchard UGV operation while handling obstacles and bounded control inputs. The abstract does not state explicit limitations.

Source: Advancing Machine Learning-Based Streamflow Prediction Through Event Greedy Selection, Asymmetric Loss Function, and Rainfall Forecasting Uncertainty
Abstract: This paper advances machine learning (ML)-based streamflow prediction by strategically selecting rainfall events, introducing a new loss function, and addressing rainfall forecast uncertainties. Focusing on the Iowa River Basin, we applied the stochastic storm transposition (SST) method to create realistic rainfall events, which were input into a hydrological model to generate corresponding streamflow data for training and testing deterministic and probabilistic ML models. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks were employed to predict streamflow up to 12 h ahead. An active learning approach was used to identify the most informative rainfall events, reducing data generation effort. Additionally, we introduced a novel asymmetric peak loss function to improve peak streamflow prediction accuracy. Incorporating rainfall forecast uncertainties, our probabilistic LSTM model provided uncertainty quantification for streamflow predictions. Performance evaluation using different metrics improved the accuracy and reliability of our models. These contributions enhance flood forecasting and decision-making while significantly reducing computational time and costs.
Methods: Iowa River Basin study using stochastic storm transposition to generate rainfall events, a hydrological model to create streamflow training/testing data, and LSTM-based deterministic and probabilistic streamflow prediction up to 12 h ahead. Active learning selected informative rainfall events, and a novel asymmetric peak loss function was introduced.
Results: Including rainfall forecast uncertainties, the probabilistic LSTM provided uncertainty quantification for streamflow predictions. Performance evaluation across metrics improved model accuracy and reliability, with reduced data generation effort and computational time.
Conclusions: The approach enhances flood forecasting and decision-making while reducing computational time and costs. Peak-loss design and event selection improve streamflow prediction, especially for peak flows.

Source: From IoT to AIoT: Evolving Agricultural Systems Through Intelligent Connectivity in Low-Income Countries
Abstract: The convergence of Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things has given rise to the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), which enables connected systems to operate with greater autonomy, adaptability, and contextual awareness. In agriculture, this evolution supports precision farming, improves resource allocation, and strengthens climate resilience by enhancing the capacity of farming systems to anticipate, absorb, and recover from environmental shocks. This review provides a structured synthesis of the transition from IoT-based monitoring to AIoT-driven intelligent agriculture and examines key applications such as smart irrigation, pest and disease detection, soil and crop health assessment, yield prediction, and livestock management. To ensure methodological rigor and transparency, this study follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic literature reviews. A comprehensive search and multi-stage screening procedure was conducted across major scholarly repositories, resulting in a curated selection of studies published between 2018 and 2025. These sources were analyzed thematically to identify technological enablers, implementation barriers, and contextual factors affecting adoption particularly within low-income countries where infrastructural constraints, limited digital capacity, and economic disparities shape AIoT deployment. Building on these insights, the article proposes an AIoT architecture tailored to resource-constrained agricultural environments. The architecture integrates sensing technologies, connectivity layers, edge intelligence, data processing pipelines, and decision-support mechanisms, and is supported by governance, data stewardship, and capacity-building frameworks. By combining systematic evidence with conceptual analysis, this review offers a comprehensive perspective on the transformative potential of AIoT in advancing sustainable, inclusive, and intelligent food production systems.
Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020, with a comprehensive search and multi-stage screening across major scholarly repositories; studies published from 2018 to 2025 were analyzed thematically.
Results: The review identified applications in smart irrigation, pest and disease detection, soil and crop health assessment, yield prediction, and livestock management. It found technological enablers, implementation barriers, and contextual factors shaping AIoT adoption in low-income countries.
Conclusions: AIoT can advance sustainable, inclusive, and intelligent agriculture, especially through a resource-constrained architecture with sensing, connectivity, edge intelligence, and decision support. Key limitations are infrastructural constraints, limited digital capacity, and economic disparities in low-income countries.

Source: iMESc – an interactive machine learning app for environmental sciences
Abstract: As environmental sciences increasingly rely on complex datasets, machine learning (ML) has become crucial for identifying patterns and relationships. However, the integration of ML into workflows can pose challenges due to technical barriers or the time-intensive nature of coding. To address these issues, we developed iMESc, an interactive ML app designed to streamline and simplify ML workflows for environmental data. Developed in R and built on the Shiny platform, iMESc enables the integration of supervised and unsupervised ML methods, along with tools for data preprocessing, visualization, descriptive statistics, and spatial analysis. The Datalist system ensures seamless transitions between analytical workflows, while the “savepoints” feature enhances reproducibility by preserving the analysis state. We demonstrate iMESc’s flexibility with four workflows applied to a case study predicting nematode community structure based on environmental data. The classical statistical approaches, the Redundancy Analysis (RDA) and Piecewise RDA (pwRDA), explained 30.7% and 53%, respectively. The SuperSOM model achieved an R<sup>2</sup> of 0.60 for training and 0.291 for testing, identifying spatial patterns across depth zones. Finally, a hybrid model combining an unsupervised SOM and followed by the supervised Random Forest model returned an accuracy of 83.47% for the training and 80.77% for the test, with Bathymetry, Chlorophyll, and Coarse Sand as key predictive variables. IMESc permits the customization of plots and saving the workflows into “savepoints” guarantying reproducibility. iMESc bridges the gap between the complexity of machine learning algorithms and the need for user-friendly interfaces in environmental research. By reducing the technical burden of coding, iMESc allows researchers to focus on scientific inquiry, improving both the efficiency and depth of their analyses.
Methods: Software development paper describing iMESc, an R/Shiny interactive ML app for environmental data. The abstract demonstrates four workflows on a nematode-community case study using supervised and unsupervised methods, including RDA, pwRDA, SuperSOM, SOM, and Random Forest.
Results: RDA and pwRDA explained 30.7% and 53% of variance, respectively. SuperSOM achieved R² of 0.60 (training) and 0.291 (testing), and the SOM+Random Forest hybrid reached 83.47% training accuracy and 80.77% test accuracy.
Conclusions: iMESc is presented as a user-friendly, reproducible platform that reduces coding burden and helps integrate machine learning into environmental research. The authors position it as bridging complex algorithms and practical environmental analysis.

Source: Integrated digital twins for agricultural machinery and robotics: A systematic review of architectures, quantified impacts, and deployment gaps
Abstract: Digital twin (DT) technology is progressively employed to facilitate autonomous field operations, predictive maintenance, and adaptive control in precision agriculture. This review analyzes 443 sources published from 2015 to 2026. The literature was categorized into 322 peer-reviewed studies, 32 scholarly preprints, and 89 non-peer-reviewed sources, comprising trade articles, commercial reports, and technical blogs, to uphold a clear evidence base. From the core corpus, 32 papers were chosen for comprehensive structural analysis, while the other studies were utilized to figure out overall trends in simulation platforms, modeling methodologies, and robotic applications. The review establishes a classification framework for agricultural digital twin systems, categorizing them according to physical and virtual twin structures and four levels of integration. Recent research demonstrates significant advancements in CAD-based modeling, photogrammetry, model predictive control, edge computing, and single-machine navigation. However, several significant gaps persist. Many systems continue to represent machinery and field environments at a rudimentary scale, with insufficient focus on crop interaction, nonlinear soil-tool dynamics, and internal machine degradation, including drivetrain fatigue. The shift from single-machine systems to fleet-level deployment is constrained by inconsistent communication protocols, fragmented data pipelines, and unreliable rural network connectivity. The analysis indicates that practical implementation relies on factors beyond mere technical performance. Limited compatibility with older machinery, high initial cost, uncertain data ownership, and the absence of certification procedures for autonomous field decisions continue to prevent deployment. Future studies should advance beyond individual prototypes to develop interoperable, closed-loop digital twin systems validated in actual farming environments throughout various seasons.
Methods: PRISMA-based systematic review of 443 sources (2015-2026) from Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, SciSpace, Google Scholar, and arXiv. A 32-paper core corpus was used for detailed structural/KPI analysis, with descriptive mapping rather than pooled statistical analysis.
Results: The review identified unified taxonomies for physical twins, virtual twins, and four integration levels, plus quantified gains in energy efficiency, downtime reduction, autonomy, and accuracy. Fewer than 10% of studies reported rigorous field-level numerical validation.
Conclusions: Agricultural digital twins are progressing from theoretical models to field-deployed cyber-physical systems, but adoption is limited by weak field validation, fragmented standards, rural connectivity, high cost, and legal/data-governance gaps. The authors call for interoperable, closed-loop, backward-compatible systems validated in real farms across seasons.

Source: Towards digital twin-enabled greenhouse management: Enhancing climate resilience and sustainability through machine learning-driven controlled environmental agriculture
Abstract: Greenhouse agriculture in the Mediterranean faces increasing demand for sustainability and resource efficiency. This paper presents the implementation of Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) solutions in the Attica region, integrating machine learning (ML) and Digital Twin technologies. An intelligent recommendation system predicts optimal settings for greenhouse microclimates, automatically adjusting components like windows and fans to enhance crop conditions. The system incorporates Random Forest Multioutput models for real-time decision support in energy and climate management. Integration with Digital Twins enables advanced analytics and simulation capabilities. Results indicate significant improvements in energy efficiency, resource utilization, and agricultural resilience. Furthermore, the framework supports the development of energy clusters through communication tools and novel business models. This work highlights the potential of ML-driven CEA systems in promoting sustainable agriculture and informed environmental management in the Mediterranean context.
Methods: Case study and proof-of-concept implementation in a greenhouse in Attica, Greece, using IoT sensor data, Random Forest Regression multi-output prediction, split-conformal prediction, and human-in-the-loop decision support. The model was trained with a 70/15/15 split and evaluated against a PID baseline.
Results: The RFR model achieved R² above 0.88, MAE below 6% for most actuator variables, and fan prediction PICP of 99.4%; windows reached 93.4% PICP, while curtains undercovered at 84.6%. Compared with the PID baseline, the machine-learning model had much lower errors and better reproduced actuator settings.
Conclusions: The proposed ML-driven digital-twin greenhouse framework improved microclimate control, energy efficiency, and resource use while supporting agronomist oversight. Key limitations were adaptability across diverse greenhouses, sensor data quality, and computational demands for real-time processing.

Source: Exploring an occupant-involved closed-loop wearable sensing system and online tuning for individualized thermal preference
Abstract: This study introduces a novel, human-in-the-loop multimodal sensing system and platform, designed for the data collection and modeling of individualized thermal comfort. We investigated whether incorporating alert-based wearable sensing and online threshold-tuning functions can enhance human interaction with the indoor environment, thereby improving the efficiency and effectiveness of data gathering for predictive modeling. The research findings indicate that the proposed method significantly reduces the number of sampling points needed to achieve equivalent overall accuracy in predictive models by monitoring the physiological and environmental inputs to the system. Likewise, for the same input data quantity, the cross-validation accuracy of the optimized models outperformed that of the baseline model. This system decreases the user's input requirements and boosts autonomous data collection and modeling on an individual basis for personal comfort modeling purposes, which can be also incorporated into long-term indoor environment monitoring and smart building paradigms.
Methods: Two-phase human-in-the-loop study with 2 subjects using wearable, environmental, and smartphone survey data. Phase I built baseline ranger models with fixed thresholds; Phase II used mini-batch (32) online threshold tuning and feature-importance-guided alerts, evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and random hyperparameter search.
Results: The ranger model was selected for both subjects. Phase II reduced required data points by about 12.8% and 36% for equivalent overall accuracy, and improved cross-validation accuracy by 5.5% and 25% versus Phase I.
Conclusions: The closed-loop, feature-importance-based tuning framework improved data collection efficiency and model quality while reducing researcher intervention. A key limitation is the very small sample size of 2 subjects, so broader generalizability is limited.

Source: Special report: The AgAID AI institute for transforming workforce and decision support in agriculture
Abstract: Tackling the grand challenges of 21st century agriculture (Ag) will require a fundamental shift in the way we envision the role of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, and in the way we build agricultural AI systems. This shift is needed especially for complex, high-value agricultural ecosystems such as those in the Western U.S., where 300+ crops are grown. Farmers and policy makers in this region face variable profitability, major crop loss and poor crop quality owing to several challenges, including increased labor costs and shortages of skilled workers, weather and management uncertainties, and water scarcity. While AI is expected to be a significant tool for addressing these challenges, AI capabilities must be expanded and will need to account for human input and human behavior – calling for a strong AI-Ag coalition that also creates new opportunities to achieve sustained innovation. Accomplishing this goal goes well beyond the scope of any specific research project or disciplinary silo and requires a more holistic transdisciplinary effort in research, development, and training. To respond to this need, we initiated the AgAID Institute, a multi-institution, transdisciplinary National AI Research Institute that will build new public-private partnerships involving a diverse range of stakeholders in both agriculture and AI. The institute focuses its efforts on providing AI solutions to specialty crop agriculture where the challenges pertaining to water availability, climate variability and extreme weather, and labor shortages, are all significantly pronounced. Our approach to all AgAID Institute activities is being guided by three cross-cutting principles: (i) adoption as a first principle in AI design; (ii) adaptability to changing environments and scales, and (iii) amplification of human skills and machine efficiency. The AgAID Institute is conducting a range of activities including: using agricultural AI applications as testbeds for developing innovative AI technologies and workflows; laying the technological foundations for climate-smart agriculture; serving as a nexus for culturally inclusive collaborative and transdisciplinary learning and knowledge co-production; preparing the next generation workforce for careers at the intersection of Ag and AI technology; and facilitating technology adoption and transfer.
Methods: Special report describing the AgAID Institute, a multi-institution transdisciplinary National AI Research Institute. It organizes work into three Ag thrusts and three AI thrusts, guided by adopt-adapt-amplify principles and stakeholder co-production.
Results: The institute defines three application thrusts: water allocation intelligence, farm operations intelligence, and labor intelligence, plus foundational work on modeling, multi-scale decision support, and inclusive human-AI workflows. It also establishes extension, workforce development, and a smart orchard demonstration farm for testing and training.
Conclusions: AgAID argues that agriculture AI must be adoption-centered, adaptable, and human-amplifying to improve decision support and workforce outcomes. Key caveats are the challenges of technology transfer, commercialization, financial barriers, and ethics/fairness in deployment.

Source: AI-powered wearable sensors for health monitoring and clinical decision making
Abstract: AI-powered wearable sensors are transforming remote health monitoring by enabling real-time diagnostics, personalized interventions and proactive disease management. This review synthesizes recent advances in AI-integrated biosensors across conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative dis- orders, mental health, and maternal/neonatal care, while addressing challenges of scalability, privacy, interoperability, and model robustness. We highlight machine learning methods—including federated learning, transfer learning, and edge- AI—that enhance the processing of physiological signals i.e., glucose levels, gait patterns, and heart rate variability. Key innovations, including FDA-approved glucose monitors and digital twins for predictive health modeling, underscore the shift toward patient-centric and data-driven care. Yet, persistent gaps remain, including device heterogeneity, privacy concerns, and the need for adaptive models that generalize across populations. Emerging approaches such as large language models and counterfactual explanations provide contextualized insights and transparent decision-making. By bridging technical advances with clinical needs, this review charts a roadmap toward democratized, equitable, and precise healthcare.
Methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, covering peer-reviewed English articles from 2014-2024 on AI-powered wearable biosensors. Searches were run in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science, with dual-reviewer data extraction and PICO framing.
Results: The review synthesizes advances in AI-integrated biosensors for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, mental health, and maternal/neonatal care. Key approaches include federated learning, transfer learning, edge AI, digital twins, and counterfactual explanations to improve privacy, robustness, and personalization.
Conclusions: AI-powered wearable biosensors are advancing personalized, real-time health monitoring and decision-making. Major limitations remain device heterogeneity, privacy, regulatory, and robustness challenges, which the authors say require adaptive models and human-in-the-loop approaches.

Source: Real-Time Automated Body Condition Scoring of Dairy Cows in a Commercial Rotary Milking Parlor Using RGB-D Two-Stream Deep Learning
Abstract: Automated body condition scoring (BCS) can improve the frequency, objectivity, and decision-making value of dairy cow monitoring, but its deployment in commercial rotary milking parlors remains challenging because animals are imaged under continuous flow, variable posture, changing backgrounds, and strict real-time constraints. This study presents a deployment-oriented RGB-D framework for automated BCS estimation during routine milking in a commercial rotary parlor. Synchronized RGB and depth images were acquired with an overhead Kinect sensor during three daily milking sessions, while RFID-triggered acquisition linked each image pair to individual cow identity. Expert reference scores were assigned using the Ferguson five-point BCS protocol with 0.25-unit increments. After quality control, the dataset comprised 25,700 RGB-D image pairs from 1,025 lactating cows. The proposed pipeline integrates YOLOv26l-based cow localization, RGB-D region-of-interest alignment, pad-and-resize preprocessing, and continuous BCS regression using a Two-Stream ResNet18 architecture with late feature fusion. Performance was assessed using an animal-wise split and compared with single-modality and alternative backbone models. The Two-Stream ResNet18 achieved the best performance, with MAE = 0.076, Accuracy0 = 83.6 %, Accuracy0.25 = 95.76 %, and Accuracy0.50 = 99.35 %, while maintaining an end-to-end latency of 95.0 ms. By combining RFID-linked RGB-D sensing, modality-aligned fusion, and low-latency inference, the framework enables automated BCS estimation under routine commercial rotary milking conditions. The resulting industrial-scale RGB-D dataset provides a reproducible benchmark for future precision dairy monitoring systems.
Methods: Commercial-farm study in a rotary milking parlor with 25,700 synchronized RGB-D image pairs from 1,025 cows. Used RFID-triggered acquisition, YOLOv26l localization, RGB-D alignment, and a Two-Stream ResNet18 with late fusion; evaluated with an animal-wise 80/20 split.
Results: Two-Stream ResNet18 achieved MAE 0.076, Accuracy0 83.60%, Accuracy0.25 95.76%, and Accuracy0.50 99.35%. It outperformed RGB-only and depth-only baselines and maintained 95.0 ms end-to-end latency.
Conclusions: The system enables real-time, cow-linked BCS estimation in a commercial rotary parlor with strong agreement to expert scores. Main limitations were mid-range BCS imbalance and single-farm validation, so broader multi-farm testing is still needed.

Source: An interactive web-based framework for scenario-driven dust storm simulation and mitigation analysis
Abstract: Evaluating long-term dust storm mitigation strategies such as terrain modification remains challenging due to fragmented analytical workflows and the absence of integrated tools for iterative, scenario-driven analysis. This paper presents an interactive web-based framework for scenario-driven analysis of dust storm variability and mitigation strategies. The framework integrates terrain editing, HPC-based simulation management, and comparative visualization within a unified environment, enabling domain scientists to draw terrain modification polygons directly on a geographic map, automatically update simulation input files, submit and monitor simulations asynchronously, and compare results through linked visualization views. A case study focused on the Arabian Peninsula showcases the framework's ability to reveal new insights into dust storm variability and assess the effectiveness of mitigation strategies. Evaluation with five independent domain experts yields a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 82.0, and all participants confirmed the efficiency of the integrated workflow. This work represents a shift from passive data visualization to an active, hypothesis-driven research paradigm to support complex environmental decision-making.
Methods: Interactive web-based framework integrating terrain editing, HPC-based WRF-Chem simulation management, and comparative visualization. Evaluated with a five-expert SUS study and a case study on a July 2018 dust storm over the Arabian Peninsula using five scenarios.
Results: The case study found the Iraq desert was the dominant dust source, the Empty Quarter mainly a deposition zone, and the Ad-Dahna a secondary resuspension source. Task 4 reduced Riyadh peak dust concentration to 4806.2 mg/m versus 6617.41 mg/m baseline, and mean SUS was 82.0 (SD 7.65).
Conclusions: The framework enables efficient hypothesis-driven what-if analysis and improves workflow efficiency for dust storm mitigation research. Key limitations are 10 km resolution, 2D-focused visualization, and dominant land-use type terrain modification; future work will add higher-resolution simulation, 3D visualization, and fractional land-use support.

Source: Cross-domain digital twin architecture for predictive maintenance via machine learning and Large Language Models
Abstract: This research introduces a comprehensive framework for creating and deploying a digital twin platform for continuous monitoring and predictive maintenance within industrial settings. Through utilizing advanced technologies, including Unreal Engine 5, Unity 3D, the Message Queue Telemetry Transport protocol, Random Forest machine learning algorithms, and Large Language Models (LLMs), we establish a platform that digitally reproduces physical equipment and translates digital controls into real-world actions. This facilitates preventive maintenance approaches and improves operational effectiveness. The digital twin platform gathers sensor data from operational equipment, analyzes it using machine learning, and delivers practical insights to prevent potential malfunctions and enhance equipment performance. Moreover, the incorporation of a web portal enables efficient monitoring and access to historical data, educational materials, and equipment status information. Preliminary findings indicate that digital twins can transform industrial equipment management and maintenance methodologies.
Methods: Case study implementing a modular digital-twin architecture across two rotor/motor testbeds, using MQTT, MongoDB, UE5/Unity AR visualization, Random Forest classification, transfer-learning experiments, and a fine-tuned distilGPT-2 LLM for guidance.
Results: Mixed-domain training achieved near-perfect to 100% test accuracy, while zero-shot transfer performed poorly (44.03% and 0.12% in reported comparisons). The LLM achieved 100% exact-match accuracy on instruction generation.
Conclusions: A modular digital twin can bridge fault detection to operator-ready action through real-time messaging, ML, and LLM guidance. Key limitations are small laboratory-scale evaluation, proprietary tooling dependence, and poor cross-domain generalization without target-domain data or adaptation.

Source: AI-enabled predictive pipelines for early warning of agricultural pests, plant diseases, and drought
Abstract: Climate-amplified droughts and rapidly spreading pests and plant diseases are eroding agricultural productivity and farmer livelihoods. Advances in Earth observation, in-field sensing, and machine learning (ML) promise AI-enabled early warning systems (EWS), yet operational guidance remains fragmented across hazards and technology layers. This study maps how predictive pipelines for agricultural pests, plant diseases, and drought are designed, validated, and operationalized—and to identify gaps that constrain real-world, people-centred EWS. We conducted a PRISMA-ScR scoping review (January 1, 2000–September 30, 2025) across the Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, utilizing dual screening, dual extraction, and a pipeline-centered charting template. From 1842 records, 72 studies met the inclusion criteria. Pipelines predominantly fused earth observation (optical/SAR) with reanalysis/forecast data, while in-situ IoT was chiefly used in field-scale pest/disease applications. Forecast horizons concentrated at 1–4 weeks (pests/diseases) and 1–6 months (drought). Baseline comparators were reported in 57% (persistence) and 39% (climatology) of studies; probabilistic outputs appeared in 38%, with calibration evidence in 21% and cross-region external tests in 24%. Operational features included versioning/registries (46%), drift detection (29%), scheduled retraining (39%), multilingual/offline delivery (32%), and interoperability claims aligned with FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) geospatial standards/APIs (25%) (18/72 studies). Pipelines performed best when multimodal, phenology-aware fusion incorporated relevant teleconnections; when model inductive bias reflected hazard physics (graph diffusion; physics-informed constraints); and when verification was decision-grade (skill vs. baselines under spatial/temporal blocks, with calibrated probabilities linked to alert tiers and cost–loss framing). Gaps persisted in external validation, reliability reporting, interoperable artifacts, and equity-by-design, and only a minority of studies assessed downstream changes in farmer behavior, avoided loss, or livelihood outcomes. A coherent, pipeline-engineered approach can move AI EWS from prototype to people-centred scale, but stronger evidence on actual livelihood impacts is still needed.
Methods: PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 72 studies (1842 records screened) from Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, using dual screening/extraction and a pipeline-centered charting template. The synthesis used inductive and deductive thematic coding in MAXQDA and descriptive evidence mapping; meta-analysis was not appropriate.
Results: Pipelines mainly fused EO (optical/SAR) with reanalysis/forecast data; horizons were 1–4 weeks for pests/diseases and 1–6 months for drought. Probabilistic outputs appeared in 27/72 studies (38%), calibration in 15/72 (21%), and cross-region tests in 24%; MLOps and interoperability reporting were uneven.
Conclusions: AI early warning works best when multimodal signals, hazard-matched models, calibrated probabilities, and operational MLOps/standards are aligned across the full pipeline. Key limitations were weak external validation, limited impact evidence, and persistent equity/interoperability gaps.

Source: AgriField-Manipur: A human-in-the-loop knowledge-based expert system for farm-level decision support under data scarcity
Abstract: Farmers must often make high-stakes decisions under incomplete data and unpredictable field conditions. Recent advances in digital agriculture have introduced data-driven and automated decision systems. However, many such approaches rely on dense sensing infrastructures, continuous optimisation, or opaque predictive models, which can reduce transparency, robustness, and user trust in data-scarce settings. This paper presents AgriField-Manipur, a human-in-the-loop, knowledge-based expert system designed to support farm-level decision-making under data scarcity. The system adopts a hybrid architecture that integrates transparent rule-based reasoning with a machine learning component limited to one-time crop suitability screening at the start of a growing season. Environmental context is obtained through low-cost sensing and district-level rainfall information, while agronomic expertise is encoded as explicit rule sets to generate advisory guidance for irrigation, fertiliser management, pest and disease risk, and soil health. To reduce automation bias, the selected crop is fixed for the duration of the season. All system outputs remain advisory, and the system does not perform automated actuation or feedback-driven control. System operation follows an interval-based execution model, allowing expert rules to respond to changing environmental conditions while preserving predictable behaviour. Evaluation is supported through a daily reflective feedback mechanism exercised under simulated seasonal operation to assess interaction feasibility and system stability. The results indicate that a knowledge-based expert system combined with a constrained machine-learning component can support transparent and practical farm-level decision-making in data-scarce agricultural environments such as the Manipur valley.
Methods: Design-and-implementation paper describing a human-in-the-loop, knowledge-based expert system for Manipur valley agriculture. It combines low-cost sensing, rule-based agronomic reasoning, a one-time XGBoost crop-suitability gatekeeper (80:20 split; 10 random splits), and simulated seasonal evaluation with daily reflective feedback.
Results: The gatekeeper showed stable performance across 10 random data splits with minimal variance (σ < 0.02) and strong recall for unsuitable cases. Simulated seasonal operation showed no contradictory advisory states, and rule-based inference remained stable under low-cost sensor noise (about ±1–2°C and ±5% soil moisture).
Conclusions: AgriField-Manipur demonstrates that conservative, transparent expert systems can support practical farm-level decisions under data scarcity while preserving human control. Key limitations are the simulation-based evaluation, no real farmer/extension participation, and no yield, economic, or real-world adoption validation.

Methods: Integrated IoT precision agriculture framework with distributed soil/environment sensors, LoRa/ZigBee/Wi‑Fi communication, cloud analytics, and ML models (RF, SVM, ANN, LSTM, regression) validated in field experiments over two crop cycles on a 500 m² plot.
Results: The framework improved water-use efficiency by 29.6%, reduced energy consumption by 18.3%, achieved 97.2% data transmission reliability, 94.8% prediction accuracy, and 1.87 s latency. RF performed best for prediction, with RMSE 1.03 and MAE 0.78.
Conclusions: The system is feasible, scalable, and effective for sustainable precision agriculture and smart farming. Main limitations were small-scale validation (500 m²), only two crop cycles, and the need for longer multi-site, multi-season testing with improved security and edge/fog support.

Source: An intelligent data-driven framework for real-time crop health monitoring using knowledge distillation
Abstract: Real-time, accurate monitoring of crop health is essential for optimizing resource use, yields and preserving environmental sustainability. However, deploying state-of-the-art AI models on resource-constrained IoT devices in agricultural fields is hindered by limited computational power, energy constraints, and intermittent network connectivity, which restricts scalability and responsiveness. Unlike existing plant disease detection approaches that rely on cloud-centric and resource-intensive models, this work proposes an integrated Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) framework that leverages knowledge distillation (KD) to enable efficient, real-time plant disease classification on autonomous robotic platforms during inspection or harvest. This framework is based on a hybrid teacher-student architecture that pairs high-capacity cloud reference models with compact, edge-optimized models for both detection and classification, suitable for edge deployment. Accordingly, autonomous robots, powered by AI and IoT, help by moving around the fields, gathering data, analyzing, and quickly detecting anomalies without constantly relying on cloud connectivity. We focus on wheat disease detection during the critical harvest season, enabling timely interventions and minimizing crop losses. Experiments on large-scale datasets show that the distilled classification student closely matches its teacher in accuracy (89.8%), while the compact detection model retains equivalent localization quality at significantly lower inference cost. The student model’s size is reduced by over 70%, while preserving real-time inference on affordable edge hardware, confirming its suitability for real-time inference on resource-constrained devices without compromising accuracy. The framework provides real-time crop health insights by visualizing affected areas of the field, supporting fast decision-making.
Methods: AIoT framework for wheat health monitoring using autonomous robots, edge-cloud architecture, and knowledge distillation for classification; YOLOv8s/YOLOv8n for detection and EfficientNet-B3/EfficientNet-B0 for classification. Evaluated on GWHD (~6,000 images) and a 15-class wheat disease dataset with two-seed experiments, TensorRT edge inference, and confidence-based cloud fallback.
Results: EfficientNet-B0 reached 89.3 ± 0.7% accuracy versus 89.8 ± 2.7% for EfficientNet-B3, and YOLOv8n achieved 89.8 ± 0.2% mAP@0.5 versus 91.0 ± 0.2% for YOLOv8s. The joint student pipeline ran in 3.97 ms per image (252 FPS); MQTT delivery was 100% reliable with 663.9 ms mean round-trip latency.
Conclusions: The hybrid edge-cloud AIoT approach enabled real-time wheat disease monitoring with compact edge models and cloud fallback for uncertain cases. Limitations include reliance on emulated field conditions/edge proxy hardware and the need for future multi-day live field deployment and curated field-collected datasets.
